    AI Overview
    The 25th Amendment, ratified in 1967, provides clear procedures for filling a vice presidential vacancy and handling presidential incapacity or death, ensuring continuity in the U.S. executive branch
    . It addresses succession (Section 1), filling vice president vacancies (Section 2), voluntary transfer of power (Section 3), and involuntary removal by the Cabinet (Section 4). 
    Key details regarding the 25th Amendment: 
    • Purpose & History: Ratified following President John F. Kennedy's assassination to clarify ambiguities in Article II regarding presidential inability and succession, as outlined in the Library of Congress – Constitution Annotated. 
    • Section 1 (Succession): Confirms the Vice President becomes President if the President dies, resigns, or is removed, says LII | Legal Information Institute. 
    • Section 2 (Vacancy): Allows the President to nominate a new Vice President, subject to Congressional confirmation. 
    • Section 3 (Voluntary Transfer): The President may declare in writing they are unable to perform duties, making the Vice President Acting President until a written declaration of recovery is made. 
    • Section 4 (Involuntary Removal): The Vice President and a majority of the Cabinet can declare the President unable to serve, transferring power to the Vice President, according to The National Constitution Center. 
    • Historical Usage: Used in 1973 (Ford replaced Agnew), 1974 (Ford became President, Rockefeller became Vice President), and temporary transfers for medical procedures (e.g., President Reagan, President Bush). 
    Benefits and Application 
    • Stability: It ensures a continuous, functioning government, preventing power vacuums during health crises or disability. 
    • Accountability: Provides a democratic, legal pathway for managing an incapacitated leader. 
    • Process: Section 4 ensures that if the President contests their removal, Congress has the authority to decide the issue.
